newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti share plunge triggers suspension.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti share plunge triggers suspension.

text.p: Shares in Italian high-tech group Olivetti went into freefall on the Milan stock exchange on Monday after a two-day suspension was lifted, forcing exchange authorities to step in again and halt trading.

The crisis-hit group's stock price slid to below 600 lire, triggering an automatic suspension in the afternoon under exchange rules limiting price movements to 20 percent either way, the stock market council said.
Trading failed to start again and dealers said it was now expected to get underway again on Tuesday morning.

Stock market regulator Consob later served notice on Olivetti to provide answers within 24 hours to a series of queries about the company's worse-than expected first-half results which revealed heavy losses.

The resumption of stock dealing in Olivetti was held up for two hours on Monday morning until Consob widened the limits to 20 percent from 15 percent, thereby allowing the shares to find a new trading level.
Olivetti's stock had last traded on Wednesday at 749.4 lire.

That was before stock market regulator Consob called the two-day halt in trading when Olivetti's recently-hired director general Renzo Francesconi resigned abruptly after questioning the accuracy of the company's first-half results.
Olivetti issued a statement on Friday evening defending its accounting practices and saying that its figures for the first six months of 1996 were in order.
Consob has said that it will continue its investigation of Olivetti's accounts and plans to meet the company's internal auditors this week.

Brokers said it was unwise to readmit Olivetti to the market without providing any more information. "People are disappointed with behaviour like this. You can't suspend a stock and then readmit it without giving any more details," said one broker.

Francesconi's departure came one day after the resignation from the board of Carlo De Benedetti, who spent 18 years as chairman of the loss-making supplier of personal computers, office equipment and systems integration services.
A top trade union official in the northwest region of Piedmont, where Olivetti is based, fuelled the mood of crisis on Monday, saying up to 5,000 jobs at the firm could be at risk.
Olivetti is engaged in a painful transition from data processing businesses to telecommunications services, seen as the money-spinner of the 1990s.
Investors were taken aback by a first half pre-tax loss of 440.8 billion lire ($291.5 million) at Olivetti, including a 200 billion provision to slim down loss-making parts of the business.
Milan brokerage house Pasfin advised its clients last week not to invest in Olivetti shares unless there was a dramatic reversal in the company's fortunes.

"We consider that the (Olivetti) stock poses such a risk that we advise against purchasing it before a serious rescue attempt is attempted," Pasfin equities analyst Alberto Rolla said in a note to clients.

An investment banker in Milan, who asked not to be named, said Olivetti could not survive without shutting down or selling off unprofitable parts of the business, in particular the ailing personal computers subsidiary.
"They have to do a lot before they have a self-sustaining entity," said the banker.

Investors were shaken to discover last week that Olivetti's traditionally lucrative activities such as office printers and fax machines were suffering an erosion in profits in the face of keen competition from the U.S. and Japanese rivals.
